fixed.before: There was at that time a shrewd man, very skilled in the art of medicine and most renowned in it, who as proconsul had with his own hand placed that crown of the contest on my unsound head, but not as a doctor. For of that disease you are the healer, you who resist the proud but give grace to the humble. Yet did you fail me even through that old man, or cease to heal my soul? For since I had become rather intimate with him and clung constantly and attentively to his conversation — for without refinement of words it was pleasant and weighty through the liveliness of its thoughts — when he learned from my talk that I was devoted to the books of the casters of nativities, he warned me kindly and like a father to throw them away and not to waste on that vanity the care and effort needed for useful things, saying that he had learned those things so well that in the early years of his life he had wanted to take up that profession as the means by which he would make his living, and that if he had understood Hippocrates, he could certainly have understood those writings as well; and yet he had afterwards abandoned them and taken up medicine for no other reason than that he had found them utterly false and, being a serious man, did not want to seek his living by deceiving people. “But you,” he said, “have rhetoric to support yourself among men, whereas you pursue this deception out of free interest, not because of the needs of your household. All the more, then, ought you to believe me about it, since I worked to learn it so thoroughly that I wanted to live from it alone.” When I asked him what cause, then, made many true things to be foretold from it, he answered as best he could that it was the work of chance, which is spread everywhere throughout the nature of things. For if, when someone happens to consult the pages of some poet who sang of and meant something quite different, a verse often came out wonderfully in harmony with the matter in hand, he said it was no wonder either if from a human soul, by some higher instinct, without its knowing what was happening in it, something sounded forth, not by art but by chance, that chimed with the affairs and deeds of the questioner.

fixed.before: For poetry, too, inflamed people's notions further, by using a diction made to astonish and bewitch, and able to induce enchantment and belief about the most impossible things; whereas one ought to be firmly convinced that the good never harms and the evil never benefits. For it is not [the work] of heat, as Plato says, to cool, but of its opposite; so neither is it [the work] of the just to harm. And surely the divine is by nature the most just of all things, since otherwise it would not be divine. Therefore this power and portion must be cut off from the beneficent *daimones*. For the [power] that is by nature disposed and willing to harm is the opposite of the beneficent; and opposites can never come about in the same thing. While these [evil ones] ravage mortal nature in many parts, and sometimes in great ones too — for, one by one, there is never a time when the good slacken in what is theirs to do — the good also forewarn, as far as they can, of the dangers hanging over [us] from the evil-working ones, revealing them both through dreams and through a soul inspired by a god and through many other means. And if someone were able to distinguish what is signified, everyone would know and take precautions. For they give signs to all, but not everyone understands what is signified, just as not everyone can read what is written, but only one who has learned his letters. It is through the opposite [*daimones*], however, that all sorcery is accomplished. For those who accomplish evil deeds through sorcery honour these above all, and the one who presides over them.

fixed.before: Therefore such precaution has seemed necessary even to sorcerers, though it does not avail at all times; for they trouble evil *daimones* [spirits ranked between gods and humans] for the sake of licentiousness. So purity was not a thing for sorcerers but for divine men, wise in the things of god, and it brings to those who practise it a safeguard everywhere: their affinity with the divine. Would that sorcerers too practised it always! Then they would not have been eager to practise sorcery, being shut off by it from enjoying the things for whose sake they commit impiety. Hence, being full of passions and abstaining only for a short while from impure foods, filled as they are with impurity, they pay the penalty for their lawlessness against the universe, partly at the hands of those very [beings] they provoke, partly also at the hands of Justice, who watches over all mortal deeds and thoughts. Purity, then, both inward and outward, belongs to a divine man, one who strives to fast from the passions of the soul and to fast also from foods that stir the passions, who feeds on divine wisdom and is made like the right thoughts about the divine, who is consecrated by intellectual sacrifice and approaches god in a white robe, truly pure, of freedom from passion in the soul and lightness of body, not weighed down by alien and foreign humours and passions of the soul.

fixed.before: ⟨For whomever⟩, then, a ray shines on the rational part [through the sun] ⟨from God⟩, for him the daemons are made powerless; for no one, whether of daemons or of gods, can do anything against a single ray of God. ⟨⟨But these are certainly few.⟩⟩ All the others are led and carried along, both souls and bodies, by the daemons, loving and cherishing their activities; and reason not ⟨having⟩ love ⟨...⟩ is, the one that strays and leads astray. This whole earthly ⎡government⎤, then, they govern through the instruments of our bodies. And this government Hermes called Fate.

fixed.before: 21. He frees a virgin from a love spell. — From the same town, Gaza's port of trade, a young man who lived nearby was dying of love for a virgin of God. When he had got nowhere by frequent touches, jests, nods, whistles and other things of this kind, which are usually the beginnings of a virginity about to perish, he went to Memphis, so that, having confessed his wound, he might come back to the virgin armed with magic arts. So after a year, taught by the prophets of Asclepius, who does not heal souls but destroys them, he came, eager for the defilement he had already resolved on in his mind, and under the threshold of the girl's house he buried certain monstrous words and monstrous figures engraved on a plate of Cyprian bronze. At once the virgin went mad, and throwing off the covering of her head, she whirled her hair, gnashed her teeth, cried out the young man's name. For the greatness of her love had turned into frenzy. So she was brought by her parents to the monastery and handed over to the old man; at once the demon howled and confessed: “I suffered force, I was carried off against my will: how well I used to delude men at Memphis with dreams! O crosses! O the torments I suffer! You force me to go out, and I am held bound under the threshold. I do not go out unless the young man who holds me lets me go.” Then the old man said: “Great is your strength, held bound as you are by a thread and a plate! Tell me, why did you dare to enter a girl of God?” “To keep her a virgin,” it said. “You keep her, you betrayer of chastity? Why did you not rather enter the one who sent you?” “Why,” it answered, “should I enter one who had my colleague, the demon of love?” But the saint did not wish to have either the young man or the signs searched for before he had cleansed the virgin, lest the demon should seem to have departed because released from the incantations, or he himself to have given credit to its words; asserting that demons are deceitful and cunning at pretence; and once her health was restored he rather rebuked the virgin for having done things through which a demon could have entered.

not_upheld.e5#2: Octavius: 'and what they do know they do not confess, to their own ruin' follows the Latin's order and is the usual reading (so the Loeb, 'to their own undoing').
not_upheld.e1#1: Aristotle HA: ἐπαυξανόμεναι is feminine nominative, agreeing with the sows (αἱ), so it is the sows that grow older; the translation stands.
not_upheld.e3#1: Clementine Homilies: συμπιεῖν is the aorist infinitive of συμπίνω, 'drink up, swallow'; 'compress' would be συμπιέσαι.
